newsitem.title: USA: Contaminated berries sicken U.S. schoolchildren.
newsitem.headline: Contaminated berries sicken U.S. schoolchildren.

text.p: A California food processor may face criminal penalties for distributing contaminated strawberries that made 153 schoolchildren and teachers sick and exposed thousands of others to the Hepatitis A virus, U.S. government officials said on Wednesday.

Investigators from the Agriculture Department, the Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control searched the packing records of the company, trying to track down where all the 900,000 pounds (408,200 kg) of the tainted berries went.

State health officials in Michigan, California and Georgia said thousands of schoolchildren would begin receiving inoculations of immune globulin, which is not a vaccine but contains antibodies to help prevent the illness.

"Protecting the health of children and families has been a top priority of our administration, and certainly of the Department of Agriculture," said Mary Ann Keeffe, an acting undersecretary of the Agriculture Department. "Making sure they have healthy, nutritious food is an absolute priority for us."

The USDA's office of inspector general was investigating Andrew & Williamson, a San Diego fruit processor that distributed the berries. If records confirm that the company imported the strawberries from Mexico, as suspected by agency officials, company officials could face criminal penalties of up to five years in prison and fines.
Companies must certify in writing that the products they sell to the government school lunch program are grown in the United States.

The firm's parent company, Epitope Inc. said it would recall 13 lots of frozen strawberries shipped last December. "While it is not certain that the lots being recalled are contaminated, we want to eliminate all possible risk to consumers," said Adolph Ferro, chief executive of Epitope.

Epitope said its subsidiary inaccurately described some of the berries as having been grown in the United States. The president of the subsidiary resigned from his job hours after news of the outbreak caused alarm among schools in a half-dozen states.
Some 25 million U.S. children eat lunches provided by the Agriculture Department program.

The suspect berries were thought to have been contaminated either in the field or at the processing plant, FDA officials said. Of that total, about 60 percent were sold to other buyers for use in various foods.

The Agriculture Department said it was notified of a possible problem with the berries last Thursday after school officials in the Battle Creek, Michigan, area discovered an outbreak of Hepatitis A among some 153 students and teachers.

The six states known to have received the tainted berries -- Michigan, Arizona, southern California, Georgia, Iowa and Tennessee -- were ordered by the USDA to stop serving the food. Another nine states and the District of Columbia were told not to use the strawberries from the company until more was known.

Michigan health officials said they administered thousands of injections of immune globulin, and Los Angeles officials said 9,000 students and school workers at 18 elementary, middle and high schools would receive inoculations.

"It's not a panic situation," stressed Dr. Shirley Fannin, the Los Angeles County director of infectious diseases. She added that Hepatitis-A has an incubation period of 14 days and the strawberries were consumed last week.
In Georgia, hepatitis inoculations were set to begin on Thursday, where nearly 2,000 students were believed to have been exposed to the virus through school lunches.
Consumer groups pointed to the news as proof that a new federal agency is needed to safeguard the nation's food supply.

"Last year there was a bumper crop of foodborne illnesses from FDA-regulated foods," said Caroline Smith DeWaal, a food safety expert at the Center for Science in the Public Interest. "Years of inadequate funding have left FDA with a food safety program that is little more than a recall agency for contaminated foods."
Some 35,000 Americans get Hepatitis A each year, at a cost of some $176 million in medical costs and lost work time.
The head of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control termed Hepatitis A a "mild" disease with flu-like symptoms, and said many people are unaware they ever have it.

Dr. Michael Friedman, deputy commissioner of the FDA, urged consumers not to panic. All the berries from the tainted lot were processed and packed in April or May last year and most had already been consumed, he said.
"Fresh berries are very safe and products made from other lots are safe," Friedman added.
